title: QR Code Phishing (Quishing) Explained
summary: Quishing occurs when attackers place malicious QR codes over legitimate ones (e.g. at parking meters, restaurants, or in emails) to redirect victims to credential-harvesting websites.
defenseGuidance: Always preview the destination domain before opening links from QR codes. Check for tampering stickers on physical QR displays.

title: Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) Homoglyph Attacks
summary: Attackers register domain names using lookalike characters from Cyrillic or Greek alphabets (prefixed by 'xn--' in ASCII) to spoof well-known brand names like apple.com or paypal.com.
defenseGuidance: Inspect the raw Punycode domain. Look for unexpected character sets or slight font rendering variations in the browser address bar.

title: Wi-Fi Encryption Standards & Rogue Access Points
summary: Open networks transmit unencrypted frames that can be captured by local eavesdroppers. Evil Twin APs mimic trusted network names to conduct man-in-the-middle attacks.
defenseGuidance: Prefer WPA3 or WPA2-Enterprise networks. Always use a trusted encrypted VPN when connecting to airport, hotel, or cafe Wi-Fi.

title: Mobile App Permissions & Data Harvesting
summary: Overprivileged mobile apps requesting background location, contacts, SMS, or microphone access can covertly track user behavior and sell location telemetry to data brokers.
defenseGuidance: Grant sensitive permissions only 'While using the app'. Routinely audit and revoke permissions for apps that haven't been used recently.

title: URL Shortener Concealment
summary: Shortener services (bit.ly, tinyurl.com) obscure the final destination URL, making it difficult for users to visually detect malicious domains.
defenseGuidance: Use a link expander tool or automated scanner before clicking shortened links received from unknown senders.
